newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Rebel leader in Sierra Leone on peace mission.
newsitem.headline: Rebel leader in Sierra Leone on peace mission.

text.p: Rebel leader Foday Sankoh returned home to Sierra Leone on Friday to explain to his commanders the details of a proposed peace deal, International Committee of the Red Cross and government officials said.

The Red Cross, which flew Revolutionary United Front (RUF) leader Sankoh from Ivory Coast to his jungle base, would return him to the Ivorian commercial capital Abidjan in time for the signing of the peace deal next Friday, they added.

"The RUF leader Corporal Foday Sankoh has just landed in one of his bases in the country. We flew him in this morning from Abidjan to the Guinean town of Kissidougou and from there to his base in Sierra Leone," a Red Cross official said.

Sankoh, whose Revolutionary United Front took up arms in 1991, told Reuters this week he was going to seek a mandate from his forces. "I am going to consult my people on this peace accord -- whether I can get a mandate to sign it."

State radio said President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who took office in March after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule, had given orders that a truce be rigorously respected to ensure Sankoh's security.

The two men extended a truce indefinitely in April during talks in Ivory Coast following Kabbah's election but failed to agree a definitive peace settlement. Sankoh has been in Ivory Coast since then but the fragile ceasefire came under strain with each accusing the other of violations.
Sankoh was accompanied by a senior government official from Ivory Coast, which has acted as mediator, and by Red Cross representatives.

"According to the request from the Ivorian government, the OAU (Organisation of African Unity) and the Commonwealth, these parties have asked the ICRC to fly Corporal Foday Sankoh back to Abidjan at latest next Tuesday," one Red Cross official said.
Government officials said the plan was to sign a peace deal next Friday.
The civil war in Sierra Leone, a former British colony, has killed at least 10,000 people, according to official estimates.
Diplomats said Sankoh gave an undertaking to the Ivorian government, the OAU and the United Nations that he would sign a final accord.
Asked to confirm remarks by Sierra Leone officials that an accord would be signed before Christmas, Sankoh said this week: "Signing is not the problem. To implement is the problem."
He cited Angola where a 1991 accord to end 20 years of civil war broke down over elections forming part of the deal.
At the height of the war, RUF rebels cut access to much of the interior and by early 1995 were attacking close to the capital. They held 17 foreign nationals hostage for several months.

Differences between the Kabbah government and the rebels over the presence of foreign troops -- Nigerians, Guineans and mercenaries from the private South African security firm Executive Outcomes -- had blocked progress on a peace deal.
But Sankoh sounded conciliatory this week: "We maintain that there is no place for foreign troops in Sierra Leone, but if we are interested in peace that should not be in the way."
